<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but CON consistently turned PRO's own material rather than merely resisting it. CON reframed PRO's Kuwait example into an argument that the world deliberately chose a constituted commission over national courts; turned PRO's terrorism-exception analogy into a preview of unpaid claimants and a creditor queue (a hit PRO never answered); exploited PRO's "under authorizing legislation" concession to show that "courts versus nothing" is false and that judicial legitimacy is thin; and pointed out that a single national statute cannot bind rival attachment rights in other forums — the allocation/queue problem PRO left standing. Most damaging, CON's pressure question forced PRO to articulate its aggression test, and PRO's answer ("manifest violation corroborated by overwhelming collective judgment") was cleanly turned into "a headcount, not a legal test — great powers are never manifest aggressors." PRO's closing responded only with a tu quoque rather than defending the threshold. PRO did land real damage: the veto-driven enforcement gap, the point that a negotiated settlement gives the aggressor a veto over its own reparation, and an excellent closing reframe that CON's own plan immobilises, pools and borrows against the same reserves with no judicial finding at all. CON's holding-versus-transferring/reversibility distinction, live since its opening, blunts that turn without fully dissolving it, and CON's securitisation figures remain asserted. CON also incurs a real execution cost: two speeches, including its opening and second rebuttal, were clipped mid-sentence, losing its final weighing lines. Netting the exchange, CON did more work damaging PRO's live route while keeping a plausible alternative on the table, so it edges a competitive debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's pressure question demanding the actual legal test, followed by its Rebuttal 2 turn that PRO's "manifest aggression corroborated by overwhelming collective judgment" is a diplomatic headcount rather than a legal standard — meaning powerful states are never manifest aggressors while everyone else can be. PRO's closing answered only with "their mechanism has no threshold at all," leaving the asymmetry largely intact.</best_rebuttal>
